messages.subject: basic summary statistics table in poppr not exported
messages.subject_clean: basic summary statistics table in poppr not exported
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I try to calculate the basic summary table for my genclone file where I could not ad stratification using the tutorial Population genetics and genomics in R <https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/Genotypic_EvenRichDiv.html>.
My geneclone file is agc.

This is a genclone object
-------------------------
Genotype information:

     398 original multilocus genotypes
     398 diploid individuals
   13960 codominant loci

Population information:

       0 strata.
      29 populations defined - Ornamental_1, Ornamental_2, Ornamental_3, ..., OR7, ID1, ID2
When I run the code below, it does not return me a table of stats per population as in the tutorial table

> agc_diversity <- (agc_diversity <- poppr(agc))

##     Pop   N MLG eMLG   SE    H    G lambda   E.5  Hexp    Ia  rbarD   File
## 1    BB 113  94 94.0 0.00 4.40 61.7  0.984 0.755 0.584 0.591 0.0493 monpop
## 2    FR 581 191 66.6 4.17 4.58 53.4  0.981 0.543 0.588 0.809 0.0679 monpop
## 3 Total 694 264 73.6 4.33 4.89 65.0  0.985 0.486 0.589 0.729 0.0611 monpop

It only returns me the list of my populations and not the table, and it on
| Ornamental_1
| Ornamental_2
| Ornamental_3
| Ornamental_4
| Ornamental_5
| Ornamental_6
| Pervenec
| Feral1
| Feral2
| Feral3
| Feral4
| Feral6
| Feral7
| Feral8
| CO1
| CO2
| CO3
| CO4
| CO5
| OR1
| OR2
| OR3
| OR4
| OR5
| OR6
| OR7
| ID1
| ID2
Error: cannot allocate vector of size 8.2 Gb
Is there a way I could my summary table for my data? I have 398 individuals in 29 populations, and 13960 SNP data/genotypes.
Thank you,
Claudia

messages.body_plain:
Hello Claudia,

You might want to consider using a genlight/snpclone object instead of genclone. If you imported your data from a VCF file, then you can use the vcf2genlight() in the vcfR package. Note that this will only work if you have biallelic SNPs.

Best,

Zhian

The documentation states the "fraction of the data to seek the threshold" but I am still confused.
An example to help understand would be very helpful too!
Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [poppr] cutoff_predictor(thresholds, fraction = 0.5)
messages.subject_clean: [poppr] cutoff_predictor(thresholds, fraction = 0.5)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

This refers to the fraction of cutoff thresholds. If you line up the thresholds from smallest to largest, normally you would expect to find a cutoff point within the first 50% of these, but in the latter half, you might find some thresholds that are separated far apart, which would predict a cutoff at a very great genetic distance, which is not great for detecting multilocus lineages.

Hope that helps,

Zhian

messages.subject: mlg, missing data, and breaking ties
messages.subject_clean: mlg, missing data, and breaking ties
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have an SSR dataset with some missing data (2.6%), for 30 populations with extreme inbreeding (possibly clonal). I want to tabulate multi-locus genotypes for each population, and identify mlg shared among populations.

I have a situation where two mlg in different populations differ only for one marker, and that marker is missing for one sample:

> tab(trichGI4)[c(11:13, 42:43), 41:45 ]
       TP80B.217 TP80B.220 TP80B.223 TP80B.208 TP80B.211
CTTP26         2         0         0         0         0
CTTP27         2         0         0         0         0
CTTP30        NA        NA        NA        NA        NA
MAMT02         0         0         0         2         0
MAMT06         0         0         0         2         0

When I use `mlg.filter` on these data, CTTP30 is assigned the same mlg as MAMT02 and MAMT06, distinct from the samples in the same population, CTTP26 and CTTP30. `diss.dist` is 0 for all the samples in population CTTP, and also among the MAMT samples and CTTP30:

> as.matrix(diss.dist(trichGI4))[c(11:13, 42:43), c(11:13, 42:43) ]
       CTTP26 CTTP27 CTTP30 MAMT02 MAMT06
CTTP26      0      0      0      2      2
CTTP27      0      0      0      2      2
CTTP30      0      0      0      0      0
MAMT02      2      2      0      0      0
MAMT06      2      2      0      0      0

I understand that CTTP30 gets assigned to the MAMT02 mlg because that mlg is ranked ahead of the CTTP mlg ("00020" ranks before "20000"). This makes sense numerically, but it would be more sensible in this case to assign ambigous mlg to an mlg from the same population, when their diss.dist is 0. How could I do this? Is there a way to break ranking ties with a different variable?

I have 406 complete genotypes, and another 100 genotypes with 1-3 missing loci, so I'd like to avoid modifying these by hand.

Best,

Tyler

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

I was initially going to suggest to use Bruvo's distance, but then I realized that it wouldn't actually do anything in this situation because you would still end up with a tie (and your data may or may not violate the assumptions). I think what you might be able to do is to take the filtered MLLs, manually change the incorrectly placed MLLs to be what you believe is correct and reassign them as custom MLLs with mll.custom(): https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/mll.custom.html

It does require a little bit of manual work, but you are not modifying your input data, only the labels.

I hope that helps. Please let me know if I did not address the problem.

Best,

Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hello Javed,

I think I see the issue here. You do not need to assign a column for each observed allele. The genalex format assumes the number of loci multiplied by the ploidy. If you have a tetraploid, then you should have four columns per locus. The LU-1 locus is in the correct format, but the other loci all have five allele slots represented. Please take a look at the Polyploids section of the manual for details: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/Data_Preparation.html#polyploids

Additionally, please make sure the header and population information is formatted correctly.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I have a related question.

I have a dataset of 237 individuals and am trying to run a mantel test on genetic ~ geographic distance. I have a SNP dataset of > 6,000 SNPs, with missing data, for all the individuals. I'm trying to figure out what method to use to calculate genetic distances.

I used stats::dist() as well as poppr::diss.dist() and compared.

I understand that the two methods are different – dist() is Euclidean distance while diss.dist() is not. However, I am struggling to understand why they are giving me completely opposite results.

Here is my code and my results from mantel tests.

The geographic distance matrix is a Euclidean distance matrix calculated using lat-long of sampling sites.

# with dist() #################################
gen.dists <- dist(allsamples.gen, method= "euclidean", diag = FALSE, upper = FALSE, p=2)

# with diss.dist() #################################

gen.dists.poppr <- diss.dist(allsamples.gen)

# check if they are correlated

mantel(gen.dists ~ gen.dists.poppr)

#mantelr      pval1      pval2      pval3  llim.2.5% ulim.97.5%
# 0.6453154  0.0010000  1.0000000  0.0010000  0.6246595  0.6667839

# geo.dists.full = geographical distance matrix

mantel(gen.dists.poppr ~ geo.dists.full, nperm = 10000)

#    mantelr       pval1       pval2       pval3   llim.2.5%  ulim.97.5%
# -0.10971653  0.99510000  0.00500000  0.00670000 -0.13648637 -0.08876814

mantel(gen.dists ~ geo.dists.full, nperm = 10000)

#   mantelr      pval1      pval2      pval3  llim.2.5% ulim.97.5%
#0.10018077 0.00050000 0.99960000 0.00320000 0.07750995 0.12707172

I also plotted the two genetic matrices against each other as well as against the same distance matrix. It looks like diss.dist() overestimates the genetic distance for individuals that were sampled geographically close to each other, which is what is driving this trend of opposing mantel's r results...

Thanks for the help!

Best,
Shailee

> rogers.dist is basically a scaled Euclidean distance (Equation 8 of Rogers 1972) whereas diss.dist/prevosti.dist/bitwise.dist* returns the fraction of dissimilar sites, but is not euclidean. The advantage of measuring the fraction of dissimilar sites is that the results are easily interpretable, but at the cost of applicability to more geometric analyses.

>
> Hope that helps,
> Zhian
